newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai air cargo sees July boost ahead of August slow down.
newsitem.headline: Dubai air cargo sees July boost ahead of August slow down.

text.p: Air freight traffic out of Dubai eased in June, but industry players are looking for a temporary boost in July before the traditional August slow down.
A Reuters survey of airlines and forwarders shows that rates to the major ex-Dubai destinations have edged slightly lower.
"The market is not very strong. Normally business slackens in these months, but it is slightly better than at the same time last year," Cathay Pacific UAE cargo manager F.A. Baig said.
An agent said he had already seen some improvement since June: "At the moment the ex-Dubai market is starting to pick up off its June low."
But others cautioned that August, again, would be quiet as many countries in Europe -- particularly Italy -- virtually close down for business as people take their summer holidays.
"May and June are traditionally soft months, in July we usually see some kind of revival and August there is usually a dip," Emirates cargo revenue optimisation manager Pradeep Kumar said.
Agents said the June to September monsoon season in India meant a slow down in production there, and a subsequent drop off in sea-air shipments from the subcontinent.
"There is not much volume, production in India has fallen because of the monsoon," one said.
Dubai relies heavily on sea-air shipments originating in the Far East and Indian subcontinent and destined mostly for Europe.

In the past few years air cargo players say the shipment of garments made in the UAE has slowed down, and traders are expecting further easing as UAE clothes factories close shop ahead of a General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) deal under the Uruguay Round.
This will wind down over 10 years the system of restrictive import quotas imposed by rich nations on textile goods and apparel from poorer nations.

Staffed by Indians, Pakistanis and people from Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, UAE clothes factories were originally set up to get around the quotas set for these countries. Once the quota system goes, there will be no need for the factories to be based in the more expensive UAE, industry analysts say.
Apart from slower garments shipments in the past month, airlines said current perishable movements from the subcontinent to Europe were good.
"There is tremendous demand to Europe of mangoes from Pakistan. We are carrying eight to 10 tonnes daily to London," Emirates' Kumar said.
He said the mango season in India was now over, but the season for mangoes from Pakistan lasted another 20 to 25 days.

Reuters calculations show the average rate on shipments to London Heathrow and Frankfurt was at 4.10 dirhams a kg, down from 4.15 dirhams at the beginning of June. On big shipments of around a tonne, the rate drops to 3.50 dirhams.

In line with the summer slowdown, rates to the United States are pretty static, airlines say. To New York JFK the average rate is stable at around 6.40 a kg, and the rate to Los Angeles is similarly little changed at 7.45 dirhams.
For heavier consignments, rates of 5.50 and 6.50 respectively are available in the market.
From Dubai and Sharjah to Baku in Azerbaijan, industry players quote between $1.20 and $1.50 a kg, depending on volumes. But one agent quoted as high as nine dirhams ($2.45) on a 100 kg shipment.
Azerbaijan Airlines Dubai cargo supervisor Nurid Aliav said rates were lower than they had been in the past few months amid a slow down in tourist trader traffic from Baku.
"The current rate, which is lower because it is summer so there are fewer tourists, is $1.25," he said.
Many Azeri visitors to the UAE stock up mostly on cheap electronics and garments in the downtown souks in Sharjah and Dubai, often for re-sale back home.
In other parts of Asia, the ex-Dubai rates to Singapore and Hong Kong were unchanged at four dirhams a kg. For 500 kg-plus shipments, rates as low as 3.50 dirhams were quoted.
East African business remains good, with agents and airlines offering rates of 4.35 dirhams to Nairobi from 4.30 at the beginning of June.
